info.bio:
12 Bar Blues es el debut como solista del vocalista de Stone Temple Pilots, Scott Weiland. Fue grabado en un receso que se tomó la banda posterior a su tercer disco "Tiny Music", y fue lanzado en 1998 por Atlantic Records. Comercialmente el disco fue un verdadero fracaso, a pesar de que las críticas no fueron tan condenatorias.
Se trata de un álbum bastante íntimo, oscuro en sus líricas, musicalmente simple y con sonidos que a ratos resultan insoportables para las masas.

scenes.name: Cantautores lo-fi de los noventa
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Los noventa son la década del cantautor: la tecnología y las redes informales del post-punk favorecen la carrera en solitario, con Joni Mitchell y Leonard Cohen (no Dylan ni Springsteen) como maestros. El folk sombrío inaugurado por Chris Isaak, Smog y American Music Club se convierte casi en un género: Vic Chesnutt, Mark Lanegan, Mountain Goats, Elliott Smith, Jeff Buckley, Ron Sexsmith, Mike Johnson, Simon Joyner, Songs:Ohia. El neo-pop de Stephen Merritt (Magnetic Fields: Holiday, The Charm Of The Highway Strip, 69 Love Songs), Chris Connelly, Frank Black, Mike Gira (Body Lovers, Angels Of Light), Richard Davies y Eric Matthews (Cardinal), David Gray. El neo-folk de Beck (folk para la era del hip hop), John Frusciante, Sparklehorse, Bright Eyes, Rufus Wainwright, Grandaddy, Bobby Conn; el neo-country de Richard Buckner y Freedy Johnston; Steve Wynn, Mike Watt, Paul Westerberg, Ben Harper.

podcast.title: Heroin Addiction Discovery (1993)
podcast.body: Following the success of Stone Temple Pilots' debut album "Core," it was discovered that Scott Wyland had become a heroin addict while the band was in the midst of selling millions of records. "STP signing their major label record deal, going on tour, and then finding out that their lead singer had become a heroin addict while the band was selling millions of records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: $6 Million Drug Spending (1994-1998)
podcast.body: In May 1998, Scott Wyland candidly revealed that he had spent over $6 million on drugs between 1994 and early 1998. "He spoke candidly of his drug problems, declaring that he had spent over $6 million on drugs between 1994 and early 1998."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Detox Attempt (Spring 1994) – Exodus Recovery Center
podcast.body: In spring 1994, Wyland intended to check into the Exodus Recovery Center in Marina del Rey for detox. He was advised against it because two other "major junkies," Gibby Haynes of the Butthole Surfers (who allegedly introduced Wyland to heroin) and Kurt Cobain, were already present. "There are two major junkies already on the premises and that will not help you kick your habit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lying to His Wife While on Tour (1994)
podcast.body: While on tour and addicted to heroin, Scott frequently called Janina and falsely claimed he was not using drugs. Despite feeling guilty about his deception, he continued his drug use. "He told her he wasn't using, which was a lie of course, and even though he felt bad about lying, he didn't stop using it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Marriage to Janina Costenda (September 17, 1994)
podcast.body: Scott Wyland married his longtime girlfriend, Janina Costenda, in a lavish ceremony held in a wealthy area of Pasadena on September 17, 1994. "And on September 17th, 1994, he and his longtime girlfriend, Janina Costenda, were married in a lavish ceremony in a rich area of Pasadena."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Wedding Life (1994)
podcast.body: After their honeymoon, Scott and Janina purchased the house where their wedding took place and began accumulating antiques and cars. "After the honeymoon, Scott and Janina bought that house, the house where they actually had the wedding and began collecting antiques and cars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Repeated Relapses and Rehab Stays (1994-1997)
podcast.body: Between 1994 and 1997, Scott Wyland entered rehabilitation facilities a staggering thirteen times, indicative of his persistent struggles with addiction and repeated relapses. "Between 1994 and 1997, he went to rehab 13 times."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rumors of Drug Problem (End of 1994)
podcast.body: By the end of 1994, rumors began to circulate widely regarding Scott Wyland's condition, with many hinting at a significant drug problem and other "dark things." "By the end of 1994, rumors had begun to swirl about Scott's condition."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Wedding Day Drug Use (September 17, 1994)
podcast.body: Prior to his wedding ceremony, Scott Wyland consumed cocaine in the limo with some of his groomsmen. "Scott bit a little coke in the limo with some of his groomsmen before the ceremony, but Emes is wedding day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Drug Treatment Agreement (May 1995)
podcast.body: Following his May 1995 drug bust, Wyland was informed by the court that he could avoid a criminal record if he successfully completed a drug treatment program, a condition he agreed to. "Wyland was told that if he completed a drug treatment program, he would be free to go without a criminal record."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pasadena Drug Bust (May 15, 1995)
podcast.body: At approximately 3:30 AM on Monday, May 15, 1995, in Pasadena, California, Scott Wyland was apprehended by police after being seen leaving the rear of a CD motel with his lights off. Officers, suspecting a drug transaction, found a chunk of Mexican black tar heroin in his wallet upon apprehension. "When they caught up with Scott, the cops found a chunk of Mexican black tar heroin in Wyland's wallet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Arrest Drug Seeking (May 15, 1995)
podcast.body: Immediately after being released on $10,000 bail (posted by his wife), Scott Wyland demanded that Janina drive him to his dealer's house to "score" drugs. When she refused, he jumped out of their 1965 Mustang while it was moving at 15-20 miles per hour. "When she refused, Scott jumped out of the car while it was still moving at 15 or 20 miles an hour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Public Statement of Remorse (May 1995)
podcast.body: While at the Chateau Marmont, Scott Wyland prepared a tearful statement of remorse which Courtney Love then called a local radio station in the middle of the night to read live on air. In the statement, he apologized to his friends, band, wife, family, and acknowledged becoming a "hypocrite" to social ideals, expressing a desire to recover and create more music. "I have a disease it went. I want to say sorry to my friends, my band, my wife, and my family and to the social ideals to which I have become a hypocrite. I ache to get well, to feel, and to make more music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rehab in Colorado (Summer 1995)
podcast.body: Scott Wyland spent part of the summer of 1995 at a rehabilitation facility located in Colorado, returning to Los Angeles by the end of August that year. "He agreed and spent part of that summer at a rehab facility in Colorado."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Seeking Solace with Courtney Love (May 1995)
podcast.body: After Janina refused to allow him back home following his arrest and subsequent behavior, Scott Wyland sought refuge with Courtney Love, who was staying at the Chateau Marmont Hotel on Sunset Boulevard. "When Jeanine refused to let Scott come home, he sought solace in of all people, Courtney Love, who had a room with the Chateau Marmont Hotel on sunset bullifard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cocaine and Heroin Charges Dropped (October 29, 1996)
podcast.body: A judge dropped all cocaine and heroin charges against Scott Wyland on October 29, 1996, having been satisfied that he had successfully completed the court-prescribed drug treatment program. "On October 29, 1996, a judge dropped all cocaine and heroin charges against Scott."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Disappearance Rumors (1996)
podcast.body: Rumors circulated that Wyland had either bolted to Detroit to attend a Kiss concert or sought to investigate whispers that he was about to be replaced as Stone Temple Pilots' lead singer (rumors that eventually proved true). "One dumb rumor was that he had bolted for Detroit so he could attend a kiss concert."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Escape from Rehab (June 26, 1996)
podcast.body: After being transferred to Impact House, a residential drug treatment facility, for what was supposed to be a six-month stay, Scott Wyland disappeared on June 26, 1996. An arrest warrant was issued for him. "But then on June 26th, Wyland disappeared."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Marriage Ends (1996)
podcast.body: His marriage to Janina Costenda ended because she "just couldn't take it anymore" amidst his ongoing drug issues and legal troubles. "And to make matters even worse, his marriage to Janina was over."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Probation Violation Arrest (April 23, 1996)
podcast.body: On April 23, 1996, police moved to arrest Scott Wyland for missing one of his mandatory drug counseling sessions. Before officers arrived, friends intervened and sent him to a hospital, from where he was transferred to the medical unit of the LA County Jail. "What actually had happened was that Wyland had missed one of his mandatory drug counseling sessions and police moved in to arrest him on April 23, 1996."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Relapse After Tour (December 29, 1996)
podcast.body: After a successful six-week tour with Stone Temple Pilots, Scott Wyland called Dean DeLeo on December 29, 1996, confessing that he had "fallen off the wagon. Hard." "Scott had called Dean Delayo at home on December 29th. He confessed that he had fallen off the wagon. Hard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Return to Court (1996)
podcast.body: Before he could be located by the warrant, Scott Wyland reappeared "safe and sober" at the Pasadena Municipal Court, explaining his disappearance as a need to speak with his wife about a personal problem. "Wyland turned up safe and sober at the Pasadena Municipal Court."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Voluntary Rehab Entry (December 30, 1996)
podcast.body: On December 30, 1996, Scott Wyland voluntarily checked into rehab once again, marking his thirteenth time entering such a facility in three years. He vowed at this point that he would get well "once and for all." "But this time, he swore he was going to get well once and for all."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 13 Days on the Run (July 1998)
podcast.body: Scott Wyland was on the run for almost thirteen days, with a continent-wide APB (all-points bulletin) issued for his arrest. His manager and lawyer refused to disclose his whereabouts during this period. "Wylandt was on the land for almost 13 days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Arresting Officer's Reaction (June 1, 1998)
podcast.body: The police officer who arrested Scott Wyland in Manhattan was reportedly heartbroken, as he was a huge Stone Temple Pilots fan and had been following Wyland's story in the press. He had not anticipated being the one to send Wyland back to jail. "The arresting officer was heartbroken. He was a huge STP fan, and had been following Wylandt's story in the press."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Continued Court Delays (Late 1998 - Early 1999)
podcast.body: His court case was repeatedly postponed, initially from December 10, 1998, to January 22, 1999, and then again to February 16, 1999, due to ongoing issues on the West Coast. "His court case was then pushed to January 22nd 1999, then February 16th 1999."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Disappearance After Bail (July 1998)
podcast.body: After his arrest in New York City, Wyland was released on bail but subsequently disappeared, failing to appear for his scheduled court date on July 31. "As soon as he was out on bail, he was gone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Disappearance from Courthouse (July 9, 1998)
podcast.body: On the morning of Thursday, July 9, 1998, Scott Wyland was last seen smoking cigarettes and answering questions on the steps of the Los Angeles County Courthouse. Upon hearing about the $250,000 arrest warrant, he vanished, knowing he would be arrested if he entered the building. "He knew that he'd be arrested the second he put inside, so he vanished."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dual Coast Legal Troubles (1998)
podcast.body: Following his July 1998 arrest, Scott Wyland faced drug felony charges in both California and New York, necessitating his legal team to coordinate multiple court dates and hearings across the country. "Wylandt was up on drug felony charges in both California and New York."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extended Rehab Stay (1998)
podcast.body: Wyland remained in rehab for an additional four months, aware that a conviction for his charges could result in up to a year of jail time. "Wylandt stayed in rehab for another four months and the whole time he was there, he knew he faced jail time if convicted up to a year in fact."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hit Parader Magazine Feature (1998)
podcast.body: Hit Parader magazine published a story with the headline "Scott Wyland in full control," highlighting a period where things seemed to be improving for him. "Hit Parader magazine even published a story under the headline, Scott Wylandt in full control."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: LA Drug Purchase Arrest (July 22, 1998)
podcast.body: At 6:30 PM on Tuesday, July 22, 1998, Scott Wyland was arrested at 6th and Burlington Street near downtown Los Angeles for simply buying drugs, rather than on the outstanding arrest warrant. Drugs were found on his person. "The police weren't looking for him because of that arrest warrant. They picked him up because he was simply buying drugs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Manhattan Drug Bust (June 1, 1998)
podcast.body: On Monday, June 1, 1998, two weeks after his solo album's release and the day before a planned New York City gig, Scott Wyland was arrested at 3:00 PM. He was picked up leaving 20 Avenue D on Manhattan's Lower East Side, a building known for housing drug dealers, where police found ten $10 decks of heroin (valued at $100 each). "They found ten decks of heroin, ten dollar packages of smack, that were worth about a hundred dollars a piece."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Missed LA Court Dates (June/July 1998)
podcast.body: Judge Larry Fiddler in Los Angeles, assigned to Wyland's case, required him to appear at court hearings to monitor his sobriety. Wyland missed a June 11 hearing (excused as he was in rehab) and a subsequent early June appearance, prompting Judge Fiddler to issue a $250,000 arrest warrant. "Wylandt missed the first hearing on June 11th, but he had an excuse. He was in a drug rehab facility."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: NYC Court Date Continuance (July 31 to November 4, 1998)
podcast.body: His New York attorney, Robert Kalina (who also represented Biggie Smalls and Run DMC), successfully argued that Wyland was unable to appear for his July 31 court date because he was in rehab in California. Judge Thomas Farber and District Attorney Christine Hatfield agreed to postpone the hearing until November 4, 1998. "Wylandt's New York attorney, Robert Kalina, who worked with rap artists like Biggie Smalls and run DMC, successfully convinced the court that Wylandt was unable to appear because he was in fact in rehab again in California."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New Management and Sobriety Efforts (1998)
podcast.body: A new management company took over Scott Wyland's affairs, ensuring he attended Narcotics Anonymous meetings. Reportedly, he was not consuming anything stronger than coffee at this time. "His new management company was making sure that Wylandt was going to his narcotics anonymous meetings, and as far as anybody could tell, he wasn't taking anything stronger than coffee."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Weight Loss (November 1998)
podcast.body: By November 1998, Wyland weighed 148 pounds, a relatively low weight for someone just under six feet tall. "At the time, Wyland weighed 148 pounds. Not a lot for a guy a shade under six feet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Last Night of Freedom" Performance (August 12, 1999)
podcast.body: Prior to turning himself in for sentencing, Scott Wyland performed what was described as one of Stone Temple Pilots' finest shows in Las Vegas on August 12, 1999. He told his bandmates, "I couldn't think of three other people to spend my last night of freedom with." "I mean, one of the last things he said to us while we were in the room alone was, you know, I couldn't think of three other people to spend my last night of freedom with, you know."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Arrest and Jail After Vegas Show (August 13, 1999)
podcast.body: Immediately after the August 12, 1999 Las Vegas concert, Scott Wyland was arrested and sent to jail as per court orders. "After the show, Wyland was arrested and sent to jail."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Divorce Still Pending (End of 1999)
podcast.body: As of the end of 1999, Scott Wyland's divorce from Janina Costenda had still not been finalized. "As of the end of 1999, the divorce still hadn't come through."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Release to Halfway House (December 31, 1999 - January 13, 2000)
podcast.body: Reports in January 2000 indicated Wyland would be released early. He was moved from jail to a halfway house on January 13, 2000, having been out of jail since December 31, 1999. "On January 13th, 2000, fans learned that he had been moved out of jail into a halfway house."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Guilty Plea and Probation (February 16, 1999)
podcast.body: On February 16, 1999, Wyland finally appeared in New York City court for his drug charge and pleaded guilty. In exchange, he received no jail time on the condition that he remain out of trouble for one full year, with any violations resulting in a 30-day sentence at Rikers Island. "That was an exchange for no jail time and on the condition that he stayed at a trouble for one full year."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jail Routine (Late 1999)
podcast.body: During his time in jail, Wyland lived in a dormitory, waking at 5:30 AM daily. He attended meetings and drug counseling sessions at 7 AM and 7 PM, had a few hours of free time after supper, and lights were out at 10 PM. He was not permitted to listen to music. "He was not allowed to listen to music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: One-Year Jail Sentence (September 3, 1999)
podcast.body: On Friday, September 3, 1999, Scott Wyland was sentenced to one year in the LA County Jail for a probation violation stemming from August 1998. Judge Fiddler dismissed letters and testimonials from friends and drug counselors presented by Wyland's attorney. "So one year in the LA County jail, Sobs broke out on the courtroom when the verdict was read."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ordered Back to Rehab (June 1999)
podcast.body: A frustrated Judge Fiddler, growing "a little tired of Wyland's face," ordered him into yet another rehabilitation facility after his probation violation. "So he ordered him into another rehab facility."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Probation Violation and Jail (January 15, 1999)
podcast.body: On Friday, January 15, 1999, Scott Wyland was arrested in Los Angeles for a probation violation. This occurred when he voluntarily appeared in court to amend his driver's privileges, and the court discovered he had failed to provide a urine sample to his parole officer to prove sobriety. He was jailed from Friday night until Wednesday morning. "Scott had failed to provide to his parole officer a year in sample to prove that he was still clean."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Probation Violation at Impact House (April 1999)
podcast.body: On June 4, 1999, Judge Fiddler received a report from Impact House stating that Wyland had been dropped from their treatment program on April 16 for non-compliance, either by failing to provide a urinalysis or by submitting a sample that tested positive for drugs. "Wyland had been dropped from treatment on April 16th for failing to comply with the program."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Relationship with Mary Forsberg (February 1999)
podcast.body: At his New York court appearance where he pleaded guilty, Scott Wyland was accompanied by Mary Forsberg, a model who was identified as his new girlfriend. "An interesting thing about this court appearance was that he was accompanied by Mary Forsberg, a model, and apparently Wylandt's new girlfriend."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scolding and Return to Rehab (January 1999)
podcast.body: After being released from jail, Judge Fiddler issued a stern reprimand before sending Wyland back to rehab once more. "And after a big scolding from Judge Fiddler, Wylandt was sent back to rehab again, then back to New York."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Accepting Full Responsibility (March 2000)
podcast.body: Around March 2000, Wyland was described as "fully accepting responsibility for where he is," not complaining or wincing, but completely owning the situation he had created for himself. "He's accepting complete and full responsibility for the web he has woven."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Continued Career (Post-2000)
podcast.body: After 2000, Wyland's career included further Stone Temple Pilots reunions, firings, another solo album, another non-STP band, and his involvement with Velvet Revolver. "There's still an STP reunion or two, a firing or two, another solo album, another non-STP band, and the whole velvet revolver thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Marriage to Mary Forsberg (May 21, 2000)
podcast.body: Scott Weiland and Mary Forsberg were married on May 21, 2000, at the Little Door Restaurant in Los Angeles during an "elucid moment" amidst their struggles. "On May 21st 2000 at the Little Door Restaurant in LA, they got married."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Noah Weiland's Birth and Relapse (November 9, 2000)
podcast.body: Scott Weiland's first son, Noah, was born on November 9, 2000. While Mary remained clean during her pregnancy and for 18 months postpartum, Scott relapsed shortly after Noah's birth, returning home from the hospital with a prescription for Vicodin after a dental appointment. "Scott was doing well too, but on the way home from the hospital where his wife had just given birth, he had a dental appointment, and he came home with a prescription for Vikiden."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Plans to Marry Mary Forsberg (May 2000)
podcast.body: Plans were in place for Scott Wyland and Mary Forsberg to get married in May 2000, despite his divorce from Janina still not being finalized at that time. "There were even plans for Scott and Mary to get married in May, despite, like I said, that Scott's divorce from Janina still hadn't been finalized."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Rehab and Jail Relaunch (Early 2000)
podcast.body: In January 2000, Scott Weiland was fresh out of jail and rehab, clean and sober, ready to relaunch Stone Temple Pilots' album "Number Four," which had been delayed due to his legal issues. He was accompanied by a minder during promotional activities to help him stay out of trouble. "At this point, Scott was fresh out of jail. He was fresh out of rehab. He was clean. He was sober."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Snowboarding with Mary (February 2000)
podcast.body: In February 2000, Scott Wyland and his girlfriend, Mary Forsberg, were permitted to go snowboarding as part of his supervised release. "In February, he and his girlfriend Mary were allowed to go snowboarding."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Las Vegas Domestic Violence Arrest (Late 2001)
podcast.body: In an incident in Las Vegas, Scott Weiland attempted to leave the Hard Rock Hotel to score drugs before an STP show. When Mary Forsberg tried to block him, he lifted her out of the way. She then called security and the police, leading to his arrest on domestic violence charges and another 30-day rehab stint. "Mary says that in a desperate attempt to keep Scott from using again, she called security, and they called the cops who had Scott arrested on domestic violence charges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Malibu Residence and STP Album Recording (2001)
podcast.body: For the first three months as new parents, Scott and Mary Weiland moved to a rented estate in Malibu, where Stone Temple Pilots began working on what would become the album "Shangri-La Dee Da." "For the first three months as new parents, Scott and Mary moved to a rented estate in Malibu, where STP began work on an album that would eventually be called Shangri La Di Da."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tensions and Fights on Tour (2001)
podcast.body: During the tour for "Shangri-La Dee Da," Scott Weiland's unwell state led to increased tensions and physical altercations within Stone Temple Pilots, including at the final show of the year in Texas on October 30th. "And because Scott seemed so unwell most of the time, tensions went up. There were fights."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Arrest for Heroin Possession (Mid-2003)
podcast.body: Approximately a month after Velvet Revolver's song "Let Me Free" was released for "The Hulk" soundtrack, Scott Weiland was arrested again for having heroin in his car. This resulted in probation, conditioned on his sobriety. "Let me free the first example of Velvet Revolver, which saw the light of day about a month after Scott was arrested again for having heroin in his car."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Arrest for Hitting Parked Car (October 27, 2003)
podcast.body: On October 27, 2003, after midnight in Hollywood, Scott Weiland hit a parked car and was arrested. He was sent to residential rehab to detox, with a judge allowing him four hours a day to leave the facility to finish recording Velvet Revolver's debut album. "While driving somewhere in Hollywood after midnight, Scott hit a parked car. He was arrested again and sent to what's called residential rehab to detox yet again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Arrest on 36th Birthday (October 23, 2003)
podcast.body: Scott Weiland was arrested on October 23, 2003, which also happened to be his 36th birthday. This incident inspired the Velvet Revolver song "Fall To Pieces." "Another big single from Contra Band was a song that Scott wrote after he was arrested on October 23rd, 2003, which just happened to be his 36th birthday."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Duff McKagan's Intervention and Martial Arts Training (2003)
podcast.body: After an initial rehab stint for Velvet Revolver's debut album didn't work, Duff McKagan took Scott Weiland to a rural retreat in Washington state. There, a martial arts expert's intense physical training regimen helped Weiland get "straight and healthy again," leading him to find his own trainer in LA. "Duff took him to a quiet rural place in Washington state to commune with his trainer, a martial arts expert who promised that Scott would work out his issues with him intense physical training."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Kicking Heroin in Rehab (Late 2003)
podcast.body: During his residential rehab stint in late 2003, which coincided with the final stages of recording Velvet Revolver's debut album, Scott Weiland reportedly kicked his heroin addiction. podcast.title: Charismatic Performer
podcast.body: Weiland was recognized as an "awesome frontman and singer" for Stone Temple Pilots, described as mesmerizing to watch perform live. "If you've ever seen him perform live, you'll know how mesmerizing this duty is on stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Charismatic Performer with Personal Struggles
podcast.body: Scott Weiland was recognized as an exceptional frontman capable of commanding large crowds with just his voice and a microphone, despite a decades-long history of personal struggles including alcoholism, heroin use (dating back to at least 1993), legal issues, and turbulent relationships. "He was one of the best frontmen I'd ever seen. Even when he was teetering offstage, few people could command a crowd like him with just his voice and a microphone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Childhood Dream of Stardom
podcast.body: At eight years old, Scott Weiland reportedly told his mother that he intended to become both a rock star and a millionaire, foreshadowing his future career and aspirations. "He remembers telling his mom when he was eight years old that he was going to be both a rock star and a millionaire."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chronic Relapse and Post-STP Decline (Years Leading to Death)
podcast.body: Scott Weiland had a long history of being in and out of rehab and jail for drug and alcohol offenses, characterized by a cycle of cleaning up and relapsing. After being kicked out of Stone Temple Pilots, his support systems dwindled, leading to increased manic episodes of paranoia and depression. In early 2015, despite his claims of 13 years of sobriety, solo performances suggested otherwise, and his managers reported seeing him use cocaine to enable more drinking. "He'd clean up, then relapse, over and over again. Now it was bad enough when he was with Stone Temple Pilots, but when they kicked him out, it looked like all his support systems were gone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Commitment to Mental Hospital
podcast.body: At the age of 16, after his stepdad discovered he was doing cocaine, Scott Weiland was committed to a mental hospital for three months following a major family conflict. "The blowup that followed resulted in Scott being committed to a mental hospital for three months."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death on Tour Bus
podcast.body: Scott Weiland died on December 3rd, 2015, at the age of 48, in the back bedroom of his tour bus. The bus was parked outside a Country Inn and Suites hotel northwest of Minneapolis, where he had intended to rest before a show at the Medina Ballroom. Police reports indicated an unresponsive male, possibly from an overdose. "He never came out alive."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decades of Personal Problems
podcast.body: Scott Weiland's life was marked by decades of insurmountable personal problems, including severe drug abuse, repeated failed rehab attempts, DUIs, jail time, mental illness (bipolar disorder), intermittent band membership, marital issues, and co-dependencies. These issues ultimately contributed to his early demise. "Behind it all, though, were decades of insurmountable personal problems. Drug abuse, the rehab stints that never took, the DUIs, jail, the mental illness, the on-again off-again membership in STP, the brawling egos and velvet revolver, the bad marriages, the co-dependencies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Drug Addiction Costs
podcast.body: Weiland openly discussed his problems, famously stating that he had spent over $6 million on various drugs between 1994 and early 1998. "He was also freely talking about his problems, including the much repeated quote that he had spent over $6 million on various drugs between 1994 and early 1998."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Drug Relapse and Solo Career Impact
podcast.body: Despite being clean and sober for about six months at the time of 12 Bar Blues' release and appearing to "have it together," Weiland was busted for drugs again on June 1, 1998. This relapse effectively marked the close of his solo career during that period. "But then he was busted again for drugs on June 1, 1998. And that was pretty much the close of his solo career."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Adulthood and Graphic Artist Job
podcast.body: After attending college for a period, Scott Weiland moved to Los Angeles where he worked as a graphic paste-up artist for a legal publication called Los Angeles Daily Journal, holding a steady job before his music career took off. "Scott W island ended up in Los Angeles working as a graphic paste-up artist for a legal publication called Los Angeles Daily Journal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Life - Birth and Name Change
podcast.body: Born Scott Richard Kline in San Jose, California. His mother, Sharon, divorced his biological father, Kent, when Scott was 12. A year later, when Sharon remarried David Weiland, David formally adopted Scott, leading him to take the Weiland surname. "He was Scott Richard Klein back then."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Trauma - Family and Personal Attack
podcast.body: Weiland experienced significant trauma in his youth. The son his biological father adopted upon remarrying was tragically hit by a car while riding his bike. Additionally, Weiland claimed he was raped by an older, bigger boy after school one day, contributing to a dark period in his life. "Then Wyland says an older, bigger boy raped him after school one day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Exceptional Stage Presence
podcast.body: Scott Weiland was considered one of the best frontmen, capable of captivating an audience with just a microphone, his clothes, and charisma. His stage presence was described as breathtaking, making it impossible to look away. "With nothing more than a microphone and the clothes on his back in his charisma, his moves demanded that all eyes be on him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extensive Personal Struggles
podcast.body: Weiland's personal life was consistently tumultuous, marked by drug abuse, car accidents, 13 trips to rehab by 1997, jail time, and domestic issues, which created significant challenges for Stone Temple Pilots. "You know, the drugs, the car accidents, the rehab, the jail, the domestic issues, all that stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Family Environment and Substance Abuse
podcast.body: Scott's biological father, Kent Kline, was described as a Pepsi truck driver by day and a frequent dope smoker by night. His mother, Sharon, secretly became an alcoholic herself, often carrying a bottle of vodka in her purse. This environment contributed to Scott and his younger brother, Michael, getting into alcohol and drugs very early, often raiding friends' parents' liquor cabinets. "Not exactly the kind of people to supervise these kids."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Financial Strain from Rehab (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: Scott Weiland's multiple 30-day rehab commitments, each costing up to $50,000 with no refunds for early departure, led to significant financial issues for him and Mary Forsberg. He had already spent millions on drugs. "Money started becoming a serious issue. When the two are finally ended, it was definitely time for a break."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Heroin as an Equalizer
podcast.body: Weiland described heroin as his "savior" and "the ultimate equalizer," using it to overcome extreme self-consciousness. He felt that while on dope, he could be "Superman" or "any man," no longer caring what anyone thought of him. "Dope was my savior, the ultimate equalizer. Or so I thought."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence of David Bowie
podcast.body: Scott Weiland's sound and vision contain "bits of Bowie DNA," indicating a clear influence from David Bowie's work. "Nirvana, the sex pistols, the food fighters, nine inch nails, REM smashing pumpkins, the killers, Scott Wyland, Coldplay. They all have bits of Bowie DNA in their sound and vision."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Introduction to Heroin
podcast.body: Scott Weiland was allegedly introduced to heroin by Gibby Haynes, the singer of the Butthole Surfers, during a tour in June and July of 1993. Weiland later claimed his first heroin use occurred in New York on August 4, 1993, following a show at the Roseland Ballroom. "It's alleged that this is when Gibby introduced Scott to heroin."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Meeting Mary Forsberg
podcast.body: Scott Weiland met Mary Forsberg in his pre-Stone Temple Pilots days when he was paid $8 an hour to drive models to appointments in a beat-up Chrysler; Mary, then 16, was one of these models. They later reconnected and became a serious, codependent couple, both struggling with drug addiction. "Scott met Mary back in his pre-Stone Temple Pilots days when he was paid $8 an hour to drive models to their various appointments and auditions in a beat up Chrysler, and Mary was one of those models."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Meeting Robert DeLeo
podcast.body: Scott Weiland met Robert DeLeo in 1986 at a Black Flag concert. Their initial acquaintance evolved into friendship after they discovered they were both romantically involved with the same woman, who subsequently moved to Texas. "In 1986, W island meant Robert Delayo at a black flag concert."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Misprescription of Geodon
podcast.body: It was revealed that Weiland was taking an anti-psychotic drug called Geodon, and the initial prescribed dosage was too high. His condition reportedly improved once the medication was adjusted. "The truth was that Wyland was taking an anti-psychotic drug called geodon. What he'd been prescribed was too much."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Music as Escape and Teenage Influences
podcast.body: Following a football injury that sidelined him for much of a season, music became Scott Weiland's primary escape. His favorite bands during this period included Depeche Mode, The Clash, Social Distortion, The Sweet, Echo & The Bunnymen, and Queen. "Music became his escape, especially after a football injury forced him to sit out much of a season."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Numerous Rehab Stays
podcast.body: Scott Weiland was noted for having attended numerous rehab centers, reportedly "almost two dozen occasions." "We could do an entire show just on the number of rehab centers where Scott Wyland washed out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Off the Charts Life
podcast.body: Even by the abnormal standards of a rock star, Scott Weiland's life was considered extremely unusual. This was evident when Slash, a rock star known for his own wild past, expressed concern for Weiland's well-being. "I mean, when a guy like Slash takes you aside and says, dude, I'm worried. You'd better take it easy. You know that you're dealing with some extraordinary circumstances."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Personal Losses and Financial Strain
podcast.body: Weiland faced immense emotional distress when both his biological father and mother were diagnosed with cancer, his mother being one of the few people he remained close to. He was also estranged from his two teenage children, with his second wife, Mary Forsberg, having full custody, causing him significant sadness. Financially, he was devastated by expenditures on drugs, rehab, two divorces, and child support, accumulating nearly $150,000 in tax liens against his property. "Then the bad news started coming again. His biological father was diagnosed with prostate cancer. Shortly after, his mother, one of the few people he remained close to, was also diagnosed with cancer. He was devastated."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Physical Decline and Multiple Medications
podcast.body: Observers noted Weiland appeared "gray" and unhealthy, relying on six different prescription medications while continuing to drink heavily. He also suffered from Hepatitis C, likely contracted through intravenous drug use. "Those who saw Wyland said he appeared gray and not healthy at all. He was on six different prescription meds and was also drinking a lot. Plus he had hepatitis C, probably contracted through intravenous drug use."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Police Investigation and Drug Finds
podcast.body: Following Weiland's death, 15 police officers and a canine unit searched the tour bus, discovering numerous prescription drugs including Nestra, Klonopin, Viagra, Dalmane, Buchenex, and Geodon. Additionally, bags of cocaine were found under both Weiland's and Tommy Black's mattresses. Black was arrested for possession but released 17 hours later without charges. "Police showed up minutes later and he was pronounced dead on the scene. It was left to a crew member to call Jamie in Los Angeles to tell her the news."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Relationship with Mary Ann
podcast.body: While living in Los Angeles, Scott Weiland was involved with a girl named Mary Ann. Their relationship was volatile, with one notable incident occurring when she became so angry with Scott that she set his car on fire. "She was with a girl named Mary Ann who once got so mad with Scott that she said his car on fire."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rock Star Transformation
podcast.body: A label executive observed Scott Weiland's profound transformation into a rock star as he dressed for a show. With each piece of clothing, he physically and mentally shifted into a different persona, ready to perform at a higher level. "He transformed a little more into a rock star. By the time he was dressed, he was a different person, someone on a different level, ready to perform, was amazing to watch."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Survival Against Odds
podcast.body: Despite a tumultuous life marked by health issues, family problems, alcohol, drugs, rehab, legal issues, and bad luck, Scott Weiland managed to live to 48 years old, a fact noted with some surprise given his lifestyle. "It was that he had managed to live to 48."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Teenage Style and Drug Use
podcast.body: As a teenager, Scott Weiland adopted a distinct style, wearing mascara and dressing in black. During this time, he also delved deeper into various types of drugs, reflecting a period of increasing experimentation and rebellion. "It began wearing mascara, dressing in black and got deeper into various types of drugs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Teenage Years and Move to California
podcast.body: After a stint in Cleveland, Weiland's family moved west to Huntington Beach, California, in 1982 when he was 14. This area of Orange County, situated on the Pacific Ocean just south of Los Angeles, became his new home. "It was 1982 and Scott was 14."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Troubled History with Stone Temple Pilots
podcast.body: Weiland was repeatedly fired and rehired by Stone Temple Pilots due to his persistent issues. "He'd been fired and rehired and fired again by Stone Temple pilots multiple times."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Undiagnosed Bipolar Disorder
podcast.body: A significant factor in Scott Weiland's and Mary Forsberg's struggles was their undiagnosed bipolar disorder, which led to extreme mood swings and poor judgment, often exacerbated by self-medication with drugs like crack. Doctors initially misdiagnosed him with severe depression, and the treatments did not control his manic episodes. "A big part of their problems coping with life is that they were both undiagnosed sufferers of bipolar disorder, and this is a really important part of our story."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Views on Heroin Culture
podcast.body: Weiland openly admitted his love and intrigue for heroin culture, referencing influences from William S. Burroughs, Charlie Parker, the aesthetic of The Rolling Stones, John Lennon's heroin period, and the mid-80s impact of Perry Farrell and Jane's Addiction. He associated heroin with romance, glamour, danger, and rock and roll excess, and was curious about its connection to creativity. "The truth is that I loved heroin culture."

xref.title: Origin of the Name "Stone Temple Pilots"
xref.body: After two weeks of brainstorming, the band settled on Stone Temple Pilots. The initials "STP" came from an old STP oil treatment can that Scott Weiland had as a "shrine" in his living space, reminding him of a childhood STP sticker on his bicycle and NASCAR driver Richard Petty, who was sponsored by STP. The full words "Stone Temple Pilots" were chosen while the band members were "drunk and stoned" as they sounded the best among many combinations, despite meaning "absolutely nothing." "From there was just a matter of matching up words to the letters."

xref.title: Original Lineup and Scott Weiland's Issues
xref.body: The band, originally formed in San Diego as Muddy Joe Young, consisted of brothers Dean and Robert DeLeo, drummer Eric Kretz, and singer Scott Weiland. This lineup remained intact until 1998, despite Weiland's struggles with drug and alcohol problems, criminal convictions, and periods in jail and rehab. "Despite Wyland's rug problems and his alcohol issues and his various criminal convictions and assorted time in jail and rehab, this lineup stuck together until 1998."

xref.title: Post-STP Project
xref.body: Formed by the instrumental members of Stone Temple Pilots after their split with Scott Weiland in 1997. "The other three guys formed a group called Talk Show".

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Probation Violation and Jail Sentence
xref.body: Starting in 1995, Scott Weiland frequently encountered trouble due to alcohol and drug issues. On September 3, 1999, he faced severe consequences, receiving a sentence of one year in the detox wing of the LA County Jail for repeated violations of his probation terms, with credit for 35 days already served. This could have been worse, as the judge might have sentenced him to general population. "On September 3, 1999, he was nailed hard. The charge was repeated violation of the terms of his probation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Producer for 12 Bar Blues
xref.body: Daniel Lanois, a Canadian producer, was responsible for producing Scott Weiland's solo album, 12 Bar Blues, released in 1998. "producing it was Canadian Daniel Landwine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Reason for Rejecting Velvet Revolver Frontman Role
xref.body: Despite the musical chemistry and positive vibe during rehearsals, Ian Thorneley ultimately did not join Velvet Revolver. The band sought a "peacock" frontman in the vein of David Lee Roth or Scott Weiland, a role that didn't align with Ian's preference to play guitar on stage. "I'm not that comfortable doing the whole, you know, front guy tambourine thing. It's just not for me."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Reunion and Second Breakup
xref.body: A year after their initial separation, Stone Temple Pilots reunited with Scott Weiland as frontman. They went on to release two more albums before ultimately falling apart "for good." "And a year later, what a surprise, STP was brought back together with Wyland out front. They lasted through two more albums before, and they fell apart for good."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: STP Hiatus Project
xref.body: During a hiatus of Stone Temple Pilots in 1998, which was intended to help Scott Weiland with his issues, the other three members (Dean DeLeo, Robert DeLeo, and Eric Kretz) formed a new project called Talk Show with singer David Coutts. This project "did not work out very well," leading to the original STP lineup reuniting. "At that point, the other three quarters of STP formed a new project called Talk Show with the singer named David Coots, which did not work out very well and STP was tuned back together in its original form."

xref.title: Scott Weiland's Involvement and Behavior
xref.body: Velvet Revolver was Scott Weiland's project after the initial breakup of Stone Temple Pilots. He was described as a "pain in the ass" to this group as well. "Wyland's next project was Velvet Revolver. He was a pin in the ass to them too."

xref.title: Scott Weiland's Last Band
xref.body: The Wildabouts was the final band that Scott Weiland was a part of before his death on a tour bus in 2015. "And finally, there's Scott's last band, The Wild abouts, and his death on that tour bus."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Scott Weiland's Personal Troubles (2000s)
xref.body: Weiland's marriage was "on the rocks," and he served an "eight-day jail sentence on a DUI charge," highlighting a period of significant personal complications. "Wyland's marriage was on the rocks. There was an eight-day jail sentence on a DUI charge."

xref.title: Scott Weiland's Post-Punk Band
xref.body: After being inspired by an art rock band, Scott Weiland formed his own post-punk band named Soy DeSant. The French name, meaning "a style of one's own," was a nod to Depeche Mode, one of Weiland's favorite bands. "That inspired Scott to form his own post punk band that he called Soy DeSant, which translated means a style of one's own."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Scott Weiland's Post-STP Project
xref.body: After Stone Temple Pilots' 2002 breakup, Scott Weiland joined Velvet Revolver as their singer from 2004 to 2008. He either quit or was fired after two albums. "Wyland went on to join Velvet Revolver as their singer between 2004 and 2008."

xref.title: Scott Weiland's Reputation
xref.body: Scott Weiland is recognized as "one of the greatest frontmen" and a "fantastic talent," but also described as a "major, major pain in the ass" due to his difficult behavior. "Wyland is one of the greatest frontmen I've ever seen perform, a fantastic talent. But he's also a major, major pain in the ass."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Scott Weiland's Response to Grunge Label
xref.body: Scott Weiland intensely disliked being compared to grunge bands, particularly Pearl Jam and Eddie Vedder. He felt that the obvious differences in his fashion sense and stage presence, which lacked any flannel, should have distinguished them. To counter these criticisms, Weiland deliberately adopted a more flamboyant, performance art aspect to his stagecraft, incorporating dresses, lipstick, and mascara. "There was certainly no flannel in Scott's wardrobe."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Scott Weiland's Teenage Influence
xref.body: Depeche Mode was one of Scott Weiland's favorite bands during his teenage years. Their use of a French name for their band inspired Weiland to give his own post-punk band, Soy DeSant, a French name ("a style of one's own"). "Remember Scott was a Depeche Mode fan and if they could have a French name, so could his band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Search for a New Vocalist
xref.body: Velvet Revolver sought a new lead singer on two separate occasions: once before Scott Weiland joined, and again after his departure. Ian Thorneley was considered during both searches. "Looking for a guided replace Scott W Island. And somehow your name came up. So let's go through that story because I find this is fascinating."

xref.title: Second Velvet Revolver Consideration and Rehearsals (Post-Weiland)
xref.body: After Scott Weiland's departure, Ian was again approached by Velvet Revolver. Slash himself called Ian to send over material, and Ian subsequently rehearsed with the band in Los Angeles, experiencing Slash's full touring rig and observing the band members as "real dudes." "The phone call came from slash. I was driving back from a gig or something. Oh, the phone rings and it's slash."

xref.title: Son of Scott Weiland
xref.body: Noah Weiland is the son of Scott Weiland and served as the vocalist for the band Suspect 208. "And finally, Noah Wyland, son of Scott on vocals."

xref.title: Three Singers Post-Weiland – Chester Bennington Moonlighted from Linkin Park; Jeff Gutt Won Online Audition
xref.body: Scott Weiland was fired and rehired multiple times; the first replacement attempt involved David Coutts in a short-lived side project called Talk Show that failed entirely. Weiland was fired for good in 2013; he died of a drug overdose in 2016 without reconciling with the band. Chester Bennington of Linkin Park — a lifelong STP fan — was brought in for approximately two and a half years, was made an official member, toured, and recorded two tracks before returning to Linkin Park. His replacement was Jeff Gutt, found through an online audition that also briefly considered John Borja from the Philippines; Gutt had been a runner-up on Season 3 of *The X Factor* and was confirmed by fall 2017. "Chester was also a lifelong STP fan since, well, since he could remember."

xref.title: Tour with Stone Temple Pilots
xref.body: Stone Temple Pilots opted to tour with the Butthole Surfers in June and July of 1993, turning down an offer to open for Aerosmith due to genre differences. It was during this tour that their singer, Gibby Haynes, allegedly introduced Scott Weiland to heroin. "So they turned that opportunity down in favor of a tour with, wait for it, the Butthole Surfers."

xref.title: Vocal Style Development
xref.body: Ben, the vocalist, initially spent the first five years of the band trying to emulate other singers like Eddie Vedder, Scott Weiland, and Zack de la Rocha. He eventually realized he couldn't sound like them and developed his own distinctive style. This unique vocal approach, combined with Ian's guitar playing, helped the band stand out from other Canadian bands of the era like Moist, Treble Charger, and The Tea Party. "I, the first five years of being in a band, you know, I was trying to sound like other people, you know, I was trying to sound like Eddie Vetter. I was trying to sound like Scott Watt. I'm trying to sound like Zack Delroch. You know, like, I'm trying to do that. And then I realized I can't do that, you know, so I just kind of ended up being me."

xref.body: Scott Weiland joined Velvet Revolver, formed with ex-Guns N' Roses members, which released two albums and toured for three years, managing "all those egos." "Meanwhile, Wyland ended up in Velvet Revolver with the ex-Gunz and Roses guys. And they did pretty well for two albums."

xref.title: Weiland's Departure and Support System Loss (Post-Stone Temple Pilots)
xref.body: After Scott Weiland was kicked out of Stone Temple Pilots, it was observed that he seemed to lose all his support systems. This loss of structure contributed to his subsequent struggles with manic episodes of paranoia and depression, highlighting the band's role as a form of stability for him. "Now it was bad enough when he was with Stone Temple Pilots, but when they kicked him out, it looked like all his support systems were gone."

xref.title: William DuVall Joins as Lead Vocalist
xref.body: Following a successful show in March 2006, where William DuVall (singer for Comes with the Fall) performed as a guest vocalist, the band considered him for a permanent role. They had known and respected DuVall for five or six years. Other candidates, like Vinny Dombrowski of Sponge, were considered but didn't fit, and Scott Weiland was deemed unsuitable due to his drug issues. DuVall was chosen because he sounded close to Layne Staley without being a clone. His integration was gradual, leading to a full commitment by late 2008. "One of the guest vocalists that evening was a guy named William Duval, the singer with a group called Comes with the Fall."
